5.2Non‐Pharmacological Interventions 5.2.1Mechanical Circulatory Support and Heart Transplantation While most patients with myocarditis have an uncomplicated course, about 2%–9% have hemodynamic instability requiring inotropic support or mechanical circulatory support (MCS) []. MCS and left ventricular assist device (LVAD) can be used as a bridge to cardiac recovery or to heart transplant in patients with complicated or fulminant myocarditis [, , ].

In a retrospective study in patients with fulminant myocarditis, patients treated with veno‐arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA‐ECMO) had a poor prognosis, with freedom from death, durable LVAD and heart transplant of 66% at 90 days [].

Data from the National Inpatient Sample between 2016 and 2019 identified 38,300 hospitalizations for myocarditis, of which 3490 (9.1%) had cardiogenic shock []. The most common form of MCS was extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. In another registry, among 850 patients with suspected acute myocarditis supported with peripheral VA‐ECMO, in‐hospital mortality was lower than in VA‐ECMO all‐comers, with nearly two‐thirds surviving to discharge []. Despite the growing use of temporary MCS in fulminant myocarditis, evidence remains limited regarding optimal device selection and timing. VA‐ECMO is frequently employed in centers with experience, given rapid deployment and effective biventricular support, yet short‐term outcomes remain suboptimal. Adjunctive LV unloading with axial‐flow devices (e.g., Impella) may reduce LV distension and potentially facilitate myocardial recovery []. Analyses of adult transplant candidates in the United Network for Organ Sharing database showed patients with myocarditis listed for transplant were younger, more critically ill, but with overall comparable survival with patients without myocarditis []. Post‐transplant rejection, re‐transplantation and survival rates were similar in patients with myocarditis compared to other cardiomyopathies.
5.2.2Implantable and Wearable Cardioverter Defibrillators

Rates of ventricular arrhythmia recurrence and mortality are high in patients with sustained ventricular arrhythmias during acute myocarditis. Although ICD implantation has traditionally been deferred to allow for myocardial recovery, the 2022 ESC Guidelines recommend ICD implantation prior to hospital discharge for patients with hemodynamically unstable sustained VT or ventricular fibrillation during the acute phase []. While ICDs have historically been recommended only in the chronic phase of myocarditis, following the development of cardiomyopathy or as secondary prevention after a sustained ventricular arrhythmia, recent studies have found that ventricular arrhythmias are common during the acute phase as well [].

In a retrospective analysis of 69 patients with acute myocarditis and documented ventricular arrhythmias during acute illness, 27 patients (39%) had sustained ventricular arrhythmia or death during a 5.5‐year follow‐up [], with initial monomorphic VT and predischarge LV dysfunction independently associated with worse outcomes. Similarly, another retrospective analysis revealed that 37% of patients with acute myocarditis (AM) had major arrhythmic events after discharge at a median of 8 months, with 60% occurring within the first year [].

Since myocarditis is a potentially reversible condition, a wearable cardioverter‐defibrillator may be considered as a bridging strategy in patients with a potentially transiently increased arrhythmic risk. In a multicenter registry of 124 myocarditis patients, the device documented nonsustained VT in 9.7% and sustained VT in 6.5%, with appropriate shocks in 2.4% and a low inappropriate shock rate (0.8%) []. Genetic variants that predispose to myocarditis can carry important clinical implications. In patients with desmoplakin‐related cardiomyopathy, the presence of left ventricular ejection fraction < 45% and LGE on CMR may justify ICD implantation for primary prevention of SCD78.
5.3Recovery, Follow‐Up and Patient Counseling

Current guidelines recommend abstinence from competitive sports and strenuous physical activity for 3–6 months, with return to activity contingent on symptom resolution, normalization of LVEF, resolution of inflammation on CMR and absence of clinically relevant arrhythmias [, ]. However, the 2025 AHA/ACC Scientific Statement on competitive sports participation acknowledges that in athletes with preserved LV function and complete resolution of myocardial inflammation on CMR, an earlier return to activity (as early as 4–6 weeks) may be considered on an individualized basis, although this recommendation is based solely on expert opinion in the absence of prospective data []. Follow‐up imaging should be risk‐stratified: echocardiography at 2–4 weeks post‐discharge for all patients, repeat echocardiography at 6 months for low‐risk stage C patients and multiparametric CMR at 6 months (or 3 months in athletes) for stage D or medium‐/high‐risk stage C patients []. Patients should be counseled to seek urgent re‐evaluation for recurrent chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope or exercise intolerance. Alcohol and recreational drug use should be avoided, and NSAIDs are generally not recommended in complicated myocarditis due to the potential risk of exacerbating heart failure [].
6Prognosis and Complications 6.1Recovery Rates and Long‐Term Outcomes

The diagnosis of myocarditis carries an overall increased risk of mortality, life‐threatening ventricular arrhythmias, heart failure and disease recurrence [, ]. In a registry of biopsy‐proven acute myocarditis, half of cases resolved within the first 2–4 weeks, whereas persistent cardiac dysfunction or progression to end‐stage heart failure may occur in a clinically relevant subset []. Fulminant myocarditis with cardiogenic shock has an estimated mortality or heart transplant at 60 days and 7 years after hospitalization of 28% and 48%, respectively []. In uncomplicated presentations, recovery can be rapid, with in‐hospital mortality rates of approximately 0% []. In a registry of 187 patients with acute myocarditis, the rate of in‐hospital death or transplantation was 25.5% in the fulminant myocarditis group vs. 0% in those with less severe presentations and after a median follow‐up of 22 months, 29% of patients with fulminant myocarditis still had an LVEF < 55% [].

Long‐term follow‐up data reinforce this dichotomy between uncomplicated and complicated presentations, with the latter carrying a ~12% risk of in‐hospital death or heart transplantation and ~15% at 5 years. Myocarditis recurrence or ventricular arrhythmias can occur in approximately 3%–9% over a follow‐up period of 19–90 months []. 6.2Predictors of Adverse Outcomes

Key risk factors for adverse prognosis include clinical severity at presentation, i.e., symptomatic heart failure, cardiogenic shock and electrical instability (recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or advanced atrio‐ventricular block) [, ]. Biventricular dysfunction consistently emerges as the strongest independent predictor of death or heart transplantation. The presence of LGE, particularly when involving the anteroseptal region, has been associated with poor outcomes, whereas diffuse LGE was not an independent prognostic marker in two recent studies [, ]. Prognosis is also strongly influenced by aetiology and histological subtype. Giant cell myocarditis is characterized by an aggressive clinical course and risk of relapse, whereas ICI‐associated myocarditis is linked to poor outcomes due to the underlying cancer and the long‐term cardiovascular risk []. Patients with desmosomal gene variants (especially DSP) had a 62.3% risk of death, ventricular arrhythmias and recurrent myocarditis at 5 years compared with 17.5% in those without these gene variants [].
6.3Potential Complications

Myocarditis is a major cause of SCD and DCM in young adults. Life‐threatening complications include sustained ventricular arrhythmias, advanced atrioventricular block, cardiogenic shock and progression to chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy []. Among patients presenting with life‐threatening ventricular arrhythmias, characteristics associated with SCD included sustained ventricular tachycardia, fibrosis involving ≥ 2 myocardial segments and absence of edema on initial CMR []. Prolonged and severe inflammation can lead to extensive and irreversible fibrosis with symptoms of advanced heart failure or refractory arrhythmias, with patients requiring mechanical circulatory or inotropic support at the highest risk. In addition, selected etiologic subtypes, notably eosinophilic myocarditis, can be associated with a prothrombotic state and intracardiac thrombosis [, ].
7Ongoing Trials and New Therapies

The treatment landscape for myocarditis is evolving, with no universally accepted guidelines due to the complex mechanisms involved (Table ). The MYTHS (MYocarditis THerapy With Steroids) trial (NCT05150704) aims to evaluate the efficacy of intravenous corticosteroid therapy in patients with acute myocarditis complicated by acute systolic heart failure or cardiogenic shock []. The IMPROVE‐MC trial is designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a 12‐month treatment with prednisone and azathioprine in patients with biopsy‐proven virus‐negative myocarditis or inflammatory cardiomyopathy, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF ≤ 45%) and ≥ 3‐months history of symptoms []. CMP‐MYTHiC is a single‐blind randomized trial evaluating whether colchicine reduces myocardial inflammation in noninvasively diagnosed inflammatory cardiomyopathy following acute myocarditis []. Two ongoing trials are evaluating abatacept for ICI–associated myocarditis. ACHLYS (NCT05195645) is a phase 2 study designed to identify an abatacept regimen that achieves rapid and sustained CD86 receptor occupancy in patients with severe ICI‐myocarditis. ATRIUM (NCT05335928) is a phase 3, randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial testing whether abatacept, compared with placebo, reduces major adverse cardiac events in hospitalized patients with ICI‐associated myocarditis. The CHASM‐CS‐RCT (Cardiac Sarcoidosis Multi‐Center Randomized Controlled Trial) is designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a low‐dose prednisone and methotrexate combination therapy compared to standard‐dose prednisone in treating active cardiac sarcoidosis []. Additionally, novel therapies targeting specific immune pathways, such as TH17 cell research, are under investigation, with potential implications for future myocarditis management (Table ). These distinct trials underscore the need for a stronger emphasis on clinical trial enrollment and for coordinated efforts to standardize immunosuppressive strategies, particularly in fulminant myocarditis, where practice remains heterogeneous and evidence is limited.

Acute myocarditis remains a heterogeneous syndrome in which prognosis and treatment are driven by clinical severity, aetiology and immune phenotype. A practical approach should combine early risk stratification with selective use of advanced imaging, EMB and aetiology‐directed therapy. Future studies should define which patients benefit from immunomodulation and identify biomarkers that reliably guide prognosis, follow‐up and therapeutic selection.

Pericarditis management has long been hindered by high recurrence rates, a one-size-fits-all reliance on corticosteroids, and fragmented care. Clinicians have navigated complex cases without a clear compass, often relying on consensus-based protocols that lagged advances in pathophysiology, imaging, and targeted therapy.

Pericarditis has a long-recognized history in medicine, with its earliest descriptions dating back to ancient times, but systematic clinical recognition began in the 19th century. The 2004 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) pericardial guidelines 1 were the first systematic attempt to standardize care, followed by the 2013 American Society of Echocardiography imaging guidelines 2 emphasizing the role of echocardiography in the management of pericardial disease, while recognizing the emerging role of multimodality imaging including cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). The 2015 ESC guidelines laid the foundation for the classification and management of pericardial diseases. As understanding of recurrent pericarditis has evolved, particularly regarding its autoinflammatory pathophysiology and the effectiveness of interleukin (IL)-1 inhibitors, the solid foundation laid by the 2015 ESC guidelines has begun to show its limitations. 3 The 2025 American College of Cardiology (ACC) concise clinical guidance document builds on the 2024 international position statement 4 and represents a welcome advance, prioritizing a precision, phenotype-driven model that leverages advances in pathophysiology, imaging, and targeted management 5 ( Figure 1 ). Shortly thereafter, the ESC released its 2025 guidelines, which recognized the growing role of advanced imaging and biologic therapies in the management of recurrent pericarditis but ultimately retained the traditional stepwise treatment algorithm outlined in the ESC 2015 guidelines. 6 This stands in stark contrast to the ACC’s modernized framework. This commentary critically examines these updates, contrasts them with the 2015 and 2025 ESC guidelines, and explores implications for clinical practice.

The 2015 ESC guidelines set the groundwork for pericarditis management, recommending nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine as first-line therapy, with corticosteroids used as second-line therapy, and immunosuppressive agents (eg, azathioprine, intravenous immunoglobulin, anakinra) as third-line options for colchicine-resistant, corticosteroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis. 3 However, these recommendations were based mostly on expert consensus, with minimal reliance on advanced multimodality imaging or phenotypic stratification. Since their publication, the landscape has shifted, with emerging evidence focusing on autoinflammatory biology in recurrent pericarditis and the role of biologics. 4

The 2025 ACC document builds on this foundation by clearly endorsing a phenotype-driven approach, utilizing advanced imaging (eg, CMR) and biomarkers (eg, C-reactive protein) to guide therapy selection and duration. 5 ACC 2025 modernizes diagnostic criteria by replacing the 2015 ESC “2 of 4” criteria with pericarditic chest pain plus at least one of the following: pericardial friction rub, typical electrocardiogram changes, new or worsening pericardial effusion, elevated inflammatory markers, or CMR/computed tomography (CT) evidence of pericardial inflammation. This elevates biomarkers and CMR from supportive to central elements of diagnosis, aligning with contemporary disease biology. Both the ESC and ACC documents introduced a tiered diagnostic approach (definite, possible, unlikely) for pericarditis; however, the 2025 ESC guidelines allow for atypical presentations in the absence of classic chest pain. 6

While echocardiography remains the first-line diagnostic modality, the ACC and ESC expand the role of CMR and CT for both diagnostic and therapeutic planning for recurrent pericarditis. CMR is now considered vital for detecting pericardial inflammation using late gadolinium enhancement and and T2-weighted imaging for pericardial edema, as well as for assessing constriction and risk stratification. CT holds significant diagnostic value in constrictive pericarditis as it can identify pericardial thickening, calcification, and other structural changes. These techniques guide risk assessment and treatment selection. 5

Therapeutic strategy has shifted from stepwise escalation to phenotype-driven care. IL-1 inhibitors (rilonacept, anakinra) are now recommended as the second-line therapy by the ACC for patients with multiple recurrences who are colchicine resistant, especially those with an autoinflammatory phenotype (pericardial inflammation evidenced by elevated inflammatory markers or findings on CMR). 5 The ESC 2025 guideline also embraces the role of IL-1 inhibitors by granting them a Class 2 recommendation. 6 However, it preserves the conventional management algorithm, in direct contrast to the modern approach adopted by the ACC, largely due to differences in pharmacoeconomics and the availability of IL-1 inhibitors in Europe.

This change is reinforced by several clinical studies 7 such as the RHAPSODY (Phase 3 Trial of Interleukin-1 Trap Rilonacept in Recurrent Pericarditis) trial which found rilonacept to be effective in reducing recurrence rates, hastening symptom resolution, and enabling successful corticosteroid taper (7% vs 74% recurrence rates in the randomized withdrawal period). Rilonacept has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the management of recurrent pericarditis, with a recommended dosage of 320 mg subcutaneously on day 1 followed by 160 mg weekly; treatment duration should be individualized and guided by clinical, biomarker, and imaging remission. The AIRTRIP trial was a randomized withdrawal trial that endorsed anakinra’s efficacy in the management of colchicine-resistant, corticosteroid-dependent patients with recurrent pericarditis (18% vs 90% recurrence rates in the anakinra vs placebo groups respectively after withdrawal). Goflikicept, another biologic, was also found to be efficacious in the management of recurrent pericarditis. Furthermore, various observational studies and large registries endorsed the efficacy and safety of IL-1 inhibitors, with the most adverse events being mild (injection site reactions or upper respiratory tract infections). These drugs are also associated with significant improvements in quality-of-life outcomes as reported in the RHAPSODY and AIRTRIP trials. This stands in stark contrast to the myriads of adverse events associated with long-term corticosteroid use as a second-line option according to the prior and current ESC guidelines. Nevertheless, corticosteroids are still reserved for noninflammatory phenotypes or autoimmune-related pericarditis. Together, these studies validated the paradigm shift in the management of recurrent pericarditis, a direction embraced by the ACC 2025 but only cautiously acknowledged by the ESC 2025 guidelines.

By preserving corticosteroids as the standard second-line therapy, the ESC 2025 guideline risks perpetuating the very recurrences, metabolic complications, and dependency that the modern evidence base seeks to overcome. 6 However, this approach is more pragmatic considering the availability and cost associated with IL-1 inhibitors. In contrast, the ACC 2025 guidance reflects a decisive modernization, one that finally aligns practice with pathophysiology.

The ACC advances the management of pericardial effusion by moving beyond simple volume thresholds to an integrated, imaging-based, and hemodynamic assessment. CT and CMR, owing to their ability to characterize effusion etiology and detect associated inflammation, are being used to guide intervention alongside echocardiography. Cardiac tamponade has been reframed as a dynamic process dependent on the rate of accumulation rather than absolute volume, highlighting the importance of coupling clinical features with imaging findings. This systematic approach ensures that pericardiocentesis is reserved for hemodynamic compromise, while inflammatory effusions can be managed medically. The ACC document stresses distinguishing transient inflammatory constriction from chronic calcific disease. With the use of advanced imaging, anti-inflammatory therapy could treat transient inflammation, while pericardiectomy is reserved for chronic, fibrotic cases. This imaging-driven classification also recognizes effusive-constrictive pericarditis as a distinct phenotype. This phenotypic approach, consistent with the broader theme of the guidance, reduces unnecessary surgery and aligns therapy with underlying biology. 5

Another landmark shift is the formalization of pericardial disease centers and multidisciplinary teams recommended by the ACC and ESC documents respectively. These specialized, multidisciplinary centers, consisting of cardiologists, imaging specialists, and rheumatologists, may streamline management of pericarditis cases. By integrating imaging, access to biologics, and genetic testing, these centers have been associated with improved outcomes and more coordinated care. 8

Despite these important advances, several challenges remain. The optimal duration of biologics remains unclear, as 75% of patients experienced a recurrence in the RHAPSODY extension after stopping rilonacept at 18 months. 9 Additionally, the role of biologics in special populations such as patients with autoimmune disease, tuberculous pericarditis, effusive-constrictive pericarditis, or patients with a neoplastic etiology is uncertain due to the underrepresentation of these patients in trials. The high cost of IL-1 inhibitors and the limited availability of advanced imaging modalities, which form the cornerstone for guiding management, could disproportionately affect underserved populations. Additionally, a lack of physician familiarity with advanced imaging and novel therapies persists. Moreover, this highlights the need for dedicated U.S. guidelines on pericarditis, with regular updates every 3 to 5 years to reflect rapidly evolving evidence. Lastly, the impact of exercise restriction is still unclear, with limited data available to guide recommendations.

Pericarditis management is becoming increasingly personalized, with the incorporation of clinical, laboratory, and advanced imaging data to guide therapy selection and duration. Advanced CMR is being increasingly used for the stratification of disease severity and monitoring. Several ongoing trials are evaluating various other IL-1 blockers in managing recurrent pericarditis. The use of wearable devices to quantify physical activity and detect early signs of recurrence may refine exercise protocols in patients with pericarditis.

While ESC 2025 guidelines provide continuity, the 2025 ACC clinical guidance redefines pericarditis management, shifting from rigid algorithms to an individualized, phenotype-driven framework. 10 Importantly, this is the first pericarditis management consensus document in the United States. By integrating multimodality imaging for diagnosis and risk stratification and targeting biologic therapy to inflammatory phenotypes, it offers an evidence-based pathway for tailored care. The evolution of pericarditis care will depend on the global adoption of the modern phenotype-driven model, which translates pathophysiologic insight into personalized treatment decisions.

Pericardial disease represents a diverse clinical spectrum, including acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, effusive–constrictive pericarditis (CP), and CP, which vary significantly in presentation, urgency, and management. Recent consensus guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology and the American College of Cardiology have enhanced clinical phenotyping, multimodal imaging techniques, and targeted immunomodulatory therapies; however, their implementation in clinical practice remains variable. We introduce our updated pathway-based framework that structures diagnosis and treatment around 5 key clinical scenarios: chest pain, hemodynamic collapse, dyspnea, incidental pericardial effusion, and right-sided heart failure. Each scenario guides a systematic process of risk stratification, tiered diagnostic evaluation, and phenotype-specific therapy. In cases of acute pericarditis, management employs a 3-tier escalation approach, with interleukin-1 inhibitors (rilonacept, anakinra) as the preferred escalation for inflammatory phenotypes unresponsive to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is integral to phenotyping, utilizing late gadolinium enhancement and T2-STIR sequences to inform treatment escalation. Management of pericardial effusion is standardized through a validated drainage scoring system that considers etiology, size, and echocardiographic hemodynamics. CP is classified into 3 subtypes: transient/inflammatory, effusive–constrictive, and chronic/fixed, each with a distinct management pathway, reserving surgical pericardiectomy at specialized centers for fibrotic or medically refractory cases. This pathway consolidates current evidence into a reproducible clinical framework designed to standardize care, enhance diagnostic precision, and facilitate shared decision-making among multidisciplinary pericardial disease teams.
Keywords: cardiac tamponade, clinical pathway, constrictive pericarditis, interleukin-1 blockade, multimodality imaging, pericarditis, pericardial effusion INTRODUCTION

Pericardial disease encompasses a heterogeneous spectrum of disorders with distinct pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and management strategies. Despite sharing a common anatomical foundation, acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis (CP), and effusive–CP differ substantially in presentation, urgency, and treatment. The evidence in the field has been limited, but recent updates from the European Society of Cardiology and the American College of Cardiology have provided structured guidance integrating clinical phenotyping, multimodality imaging, inflammatory biomarkers, and targeted immunomodulatory therapies. 1 , 2 In this chapter, we outline a unified, pathway-based approach to the diagnosis and management of pericardial disease (Fig. 1 ), building on the original CHASER framework and incorporating contemporary evidence. 3

Figure 1. Open in a new tab Contemporary pericardial disease pathway. HOW TO USE THE PATHWAY Entering the Pathway Despite the broad range of pericardial pathologies, a limited number of clinical presentations prompt clinical suspicion for pericardial disease. The CHASER II pathway assigns each presentation its own entry point, initiating a defined sequence of clinical evaluation, diagnostic workup, and management. There are 5 entry points (Fig. 2 ): Figure 2. Open in a new tab Clinical presentation pathway for pericardial disease.

Chest pain. Acute pleuritic chest pain is the most common entry point and routes the clinician to the pericarditis arm. Evaluation proceeds through clinical scoring, risk stratification, tiered laboratory and imaging workup, and a 3-step Treatment Escalation Staircase guided by inflammatory phenotype.

Hypotension, syncope, or pulseless electrical activity arrest. Hemodynamic collapse in the context of a known or suspected pericardial process routes immediately to the acute tamponade arm. Management and diagnosis occur in parallel; the priority is bedside echocardiography and urgent drainage. High-risk etiologies that require surgical rather than needle drainage must be assessed simultaneously.

Dyspnea. Exertional or resting dyspnea without hemodynamic collapse routes to the subacute effusion arm. Echocardiography establishes effusion size and hemodynamic burden; a standardized scoring system then guides the drainage decision. Post-drainage evaluation is mandatory to detect effusive–constrictive physiology. Incidental pericardial effusion. An effusion discovered on imaging performed for another indication routes to a parallel branch of the effusion arm. Systematic etiologic evaluation is performed; small effusions with normal inflammatory markers and no hemodynamic compromise may be managed conservatively with serial imaging.

Right-predominant heart failure. An insidious syndrome of dyspnea and fatigue accompanied by elevated jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema, ascites, and clear lung fields leads to the CP arm. After echocardiographic confirmation of constrictive physiology, multimodality imaging determines the inflammatory state and subtype, which guide management: anti-inflammatory therapy for transient or effusive–constrictive disease, or referral for pericardiectomy for chronic fixed constriction. 1. CHEST PAIN: ACUTE PERICARDITIS Presentation and Diagnosis

Acute pericarditis accounts for approximately 0.1% of all hospital admissions and 0.2% of emergency cardiovascular admissions. 4 , 5 It predominantly affects males aged 16–65 years, though recurrent pericarditis is more frequent in women. In developed regions, most cases are idiopathic or viral; in endemic regions, tuberculosis remains the leading identifiable cause.

Diagnosis is based on pleuritic chest pain or an equivalent suggestive clinical presentation plus objective supportive finding. Additional diagnostic features include pericardial friction rub, typical electrocardiographic (ECG) changes with diffuse ST-segment elevation and/or PR-segment depression (Table 1 ), elevated inflammatory biomarkers such as CRP or ESR, new or worsening pericardial effusion, or imaging evidence of pericardial inflammation, preferably by cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR). One additional feature supports possible pericarditis, whereas 2 or more additional features support a definite diagnosis (Fig. 3 ). Table 1. ECG Features of Acute Pericarditis Stage

Timeline Electrocardiographic Features Stage 1 Hours to few days Diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression (saddle-shaped; most leads) Stage 2 End of week 1 to week 2 Normalization of ST- and PR-segment changes Stage 3 Week 2 to week 3 Diffuse T-wave inversion Stage 4 Week 3 onwards (up to months) Normalization of T-wave changes (may persist for months) Open in a new tab

The 4 stages of acute pericarditis evolve over a period of weeks. They are classically described but are not always sequentially observed and may be incomplete or absent, particularly in recurrent or subacute pericarditis. ECG changes should be interpreted in the clinical context and are considered a supportive diagnostic feature rather than a required component. Figure 3. Open in a new tab Diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis.

While acute pericarditis represents a new-onset event, accurate classification of the temporal course is important to guide management. Incessant pericarditis is defined as persistent symptoms lasting >4–6 weeks without remission. Recurrent pericarditis involves relapse after a symptom-free interval of ≥4–6 weeks. Chronic pericarditis refers to symptoms or objective evidence of disease lasting >3 months. This pathway emphasizes phenotype-based management, distinguishing inflammatory from noninflammatory disease, which has direct therapeutic implications. Risk Stratification and Admission

The first branch point after diagnosis is risk stratification. Patients with any of the features listed in Table 2 should be admitted for inpatient management and expedited workup. 6 Table 2. High-Risk Features Warranting Hospital Admission High-Risk Features Warranting Admission • Fever >38°C • Uncontrolled pain • Large pericardial effusion (>2 cm) or cardiac tamponade • Immunocompromised status • Traumatic or iatrogenic etiology • Concurrent oral anticoagulation therapy • Subacute onset or failure to respond to NSAIDs within 1 week • Elevated troponin (myocardial involvement/ myopericarditis) Open in a new tab Adapted from Imazio M et al. 6 . Diagnostic Workup: Tiered Approach

All patients presenting with suspected acute pericarditis should complete Tier 1 testing: electrocardiography, complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, CRP, ESR, cardiac troponin, chest radiograph, and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). Elevated troponin suggests myocardial involvement and warrants further evaluation with CMR with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and T2-Short Tau Inversion Recovery (T2-STIR) sequences, when appropriate. Pericardial LGE supports the presence of pericardial inflammation and has prognostic value for recurrence. 7

Tier 2 testing is reserved for patients with persistent or atypical presentations, high-risk features, or failure to respond to initial therapy within 1 week. It includes immunologic and infectious serologies [antinuclear antibody (ANA), autoantibodies, PPD/Quantiferon-TB Gold, HIV, blood cultures], endocrine evaluation (TSH), CMR, and chest computed tomography (CT). This 2-tiered structure avoids indiscriminate testing while ensuring that treatable systemic causes, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, and malignancy are identified in those with higher pretest probability. 7

Echocardiography is the primary imaging modality. It confirms the presence and size of effusion (present in 50–65% of cases) and excludes hemodynamic compromise. 2 When myocardial involvement is suspected, wall motion abnormalities or reduced left ventricular (LV) function may be observed. CMR provides objective evidence of pericardial inflammation through LGE and edema-sensitive T2-weighted sequences and should be considered in patients with diagnostic uncertainty, recurrent or persistent symptoms, suspected complications, or when escalation of therapy is being contemplated. T2-weighted imaging reflects active inflammation, whereas LGE may persist beyond clinical improvement and should be interpreted in the clinical context.
Management: Treatment Escalation Staircase Management follows a 3-step escalation staircase: Step 1 (all patients, foundational therapy):

Initiate nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (ibuprofen 600–800 mg every 8 hours, or aspirin 500–1000 mg every 8 hours) in combination with colchicine (0.6 mg twice daily; 0.6 mg once daily for weight <70 kg, severe renal/hepatic impairment) and appropriate gastroprotection. Colchicine is recommended for 3 months in acute cases and 6–12 months in recurrent cases, with NSAID tapering guided by CRP normalization. 8 NSAID selection and dosing should account for renal function, heart failure, bleeding risk, and concomitant medications, while colchicine dosing should be adjusted for renal or hepatic impairment and potential drug–drug interactions.

Exercise restriction is recommended for at least 1 month, with a target heart rate <100 beats per minute; return to activity should follow clinical remission, including resolution of symptoms and normalization of inflammatory markers. In patients with myocardial involvement, return to activity should also require normalization of troponin, recovery of ventricular function, and absence of clinically significant arrhythmias. In selected patients, particularly those with prior myocardial involvement, persistent symptoms, or athletes returning to higher levels of exertion, exercise stress testing or cardiopulmonary exercise testing may be considered to assess functional recovery before resumption of full activity. 9 Corticosteroids should be avoided as initial therapy, due to their association with increased recurrence risk.
Step 2 (phenotype-directed escalation):

CMR should be considered before escalating therapy. For patients with an inflammatory phenotype (fever, elevated CRP, and/or CMR evidence of pericardial inflammation), anti-interleukin-1 (anti-IL-1) therapy is preferred over corticosteroid escalation when feasible. Rilonacept, a weekly IL-1α and IL-1β cytokine trap evaluated in the phase 3 RHAPSODY trial of recurrent pericarditis, significantly reduced recurrence risk compared with placebo and enabled withdrawal of background anti-inflammatory therapy, including colchicine and corticosteroids. It is the only U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved therapy for recurrent pericarditis. 10 – 12 Anakinra is an alternative IL-1 receptor antagonist with randomized evidence in colchicine-resistant and corticosteroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis. 13 For patients with a noninflammatory or autoimmune phenotype, low- to medium-dose corticosteroids with a gradual taper are appropriate.

Optimal anti-IL-1 treatment duration remains to be defined. RHAPSODY long-term extension data demonstrate sustained recurrence suppression with continued rilonacept therapy beyond 18 months, while recurrence after treatment suspension identifies patients with persistent underlying disease activity. Real-world tapering data suggest that dose-interval extension is feasible, although recurrent symptoms during tapering are common and may require individualized adjustment of dosing intervals rather than complete discontinuation. These findings support prolonged, phenotype-guided therapy in selected patients, with tapering guided by symptoms, inflammatory biomarkers, and imaging remission. 10 , 14 Before initiation of anti-IL-1 therapy, patients should be screened for active infection and for tuberculosis, hepatitis B/C, and HIV as clinically appropriate, and vaccinations should be updated.

Step 3 (refractory or recurrent disease): Patients with disease refractory to steps 1 and 2 should be referred to a Pericardial Disease Center for multidisciplinary evaluation by cardiology, rheumatology, and cardiac surgery. Radical pericardiectomy at a high-volume surgical center may be considered in carefully selected patients with medically refractory recurrent pericarditis or persistent constrictive physiology despite appropriate medical therapy. Alternative immunosuppressive agents (azathioprine, intravenous immunoglobulin) may be considered when colchicine and anti-IL-1 therapy have both failed. 12

During active disease, CRP should be reassessed serially until normalization and used to guide anti-inflammatory therapy and tapering; during stable remission, periodic monitoring every 6–12 months is reasonable. Objective heart rate monitoring may be used to guide a graded return to activity, particularly in patients with recurrent disease or athletes, but evidence for wearable-guided strategies in pericarditis is limited, and clinical and inflammatory remission should remain the primary determinants of activity progression. In contrast to pericarditis, pericardial effusion and tamponade represent hemodynamic manifestations of pericardial disease.

2. HYPOTENSION, SYNCOPE, OR PULSELESS ELECTRICAL ACTIVITY ARREST: ACUTE CARDIAC TAMPONADE Presentation Cardiac tamponade arises when progressive accumulation of pericardial fluid raises intrapericardial pressure to a level that impairs ventricular filling, reduces stroke volume, and compromises systemic perfusion. Presentation ranges from acute hemodynamic collapse, as in aortic dissection or traumatic hemopericardium, to a subacute course of dyspnea, chest pressure, and syncope, as in neoplastic pericarditis. The classic triad of hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds (Beck triad) is present in a minority of cases and should not be required for diagnosis.

Tamponade should be suspected in any patient with unexplained hypotension, syncope, or pulseless electrical activity. Table 3 lists high-risk conditions commonly associated with acute tamponade that should be specifically considered. 15 Table 3. High-Risk Conditions Associated with Cardiac Tamponade High-Risk Conditions Associated with Tamponade • Aortic dissection • Purulent pericarditis • Blunt or penetrating chest trauma • Recent cardiac procedure or electrophysiology intervention • Cardiac surgery (postoperative) • Neoplastic pericarditis (malignant effusion) • HIV/immunocompromised status • Advanced renal failure • Suspected tuberculosis Open in a new tab

Adapted from Imazio M et al. 16 . Physical Examination and ECG Physical examination should focus on pulsus paradoxus (>10 mm Hg inspiratory drop in systolic pressure), jugular venous distension, and lung auscultation (clear lung fields). Tachycardia is common, although it may be absent or blunted in patients receiving rate-limiting medications or in advanced or atypical presentations. ECG findings include sinus tachycardia, low-voltage QRS complexes, and electrical alternans. The latter reflects beat-to-beat variation in cardiac position within a large pericardial effusion and raises concern for tamponade in the appropriate clinical context. Echocardiographic Assessment

Echocardiography is the cornerstone of diagnosis and should be performed immediately at the bedside. The following echocardiographic findings support tamponade physiology in the appropriate clinical context: Right atrial (RA) collapse lasting more than one-third of the cardiac cycle (most sensitive; low specificity if only brief buckling). Right ventricular (RV) diastolic collapse (specific for hemodynamic compromise; less sensitive than RA collapse; reduced sensitivity in RV hypertrophy and pulmonary hypertension). Inferior vena cava (IVC) plethora with <50% inspiratory collapse.

Respiratory variation in mitral valve (MV) inflow velocity >30% and tricuspid valve inflow >60% (ventricular interdependence). The combination of chamber collapse with corroborating hemodynamic findings provides high sensitivity and specificity for tamponade. Left-sided chamber collapse is a late and specific finding. Loculated or posterior effusions, particularly postcardiac surgery, may not be detected by standard transthoracic windows. Transesophageal echocardiography or CT may be considered in such cases. Management

Acute tamponade with hemodynamic compromise requires immediate pericardiocentesis. The etiology determines the drainage approach: surgical intervention is required for aortic dissection, purulent pericarditis, and traumatic hemopericardium. Echo-guided pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid or para-apical approach) is appropriate for most other causes. In suspected aortic dissection, pericardiocentesis should generally be avoided, and if performed in extremis, limited drainage may be considered only as a temporizing measure while arranging definitive surgical management. 16 , 17 Fluid analysis should include cell count, protein, lactate dehydrogenase, cytology, culture, and targeted assays based on clinical suspicion (adenosine deaminase for tuberculosis; flow cytometry for lymphoma). Volume expansion and vasopressors may provide temporary hemodynamic support but are not substitutes for drainage. 18

Following drainage, right atrial pressure should be reassessed. Persistent elevation of right atrial pressure after pericardial drainage, together with persistent echocardiographic or hemodynamic features of constriction (such as respirophasic septal shift, annulus reversus, hepatic vein expiratory diastolic flow reversal, or ventricular discordance on invasive hemodynamics), should raise suspicion for effusive–CP and prompt further evaluation, including assessment for active pericardial inflammation on CMR. Management should be guided by the presence of inflammation, with anti-inflammatory therapy for inflammatory disease and consideration of pericardiectomy if constriction persists despite medical therapy.

3. DYSPNEA: PERICARDIAL EFFUSION Presentation and Evaluation Patients with significant pericardial effusion and subacute tamponade often present with dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance, chest pressure, and fatigue. Although the differential diagnosis of dyspnea is broad, pericardial effusion should always be considered. Effusion size is categorized by echocardiographic measurement at end-diastole: small (<1.0 cm), moderate (1.0–2.0 cm), large (>2.0 cm), and very large (>2.5 cm). Approximately half of all pericardial effusions are idiopathic; Table 4 outlines the principal etiologic categories. Table 4. Viral (enteroviruses, adenovirus, EBV, CMV, HIV); tuberculous; purulent (bacterial) Autoimmune/inflammatory Systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease Neoplastic Primary (mesothelioma, sarcoma); metastatic (lung, breast, lymphoma, melanoma) Postcardiac injury Post-myocardial infarction (Dressler syndrome), postcardiotomy, postablation, post-TAVI Metabolic Uremia, hypothyroidism Traumatic/iatrogenic Blunt trauma, aortic dissection, device implant, cardiac procedure Idiopathic ~50% of all pericardial effusions; diagnosis of exclusion Open in a new tab
CMV indicates cytomegalovirus; EBV, Epstein–Barr virus; TAVI, transcatheter aortic valve implantation. Adapted from Imazio M et al. 16 . Acute versus Subacute Tamponade

The clinical presentation of tamponade is determined as much by the rate of fluid accumulation as by the absolute size of the effusion. Acute tamponade, as in traumatic hemopericardium or aortic dissection, may occur with relatively small effusions (100–200 mL) because the pericardium has not had time to stretch; these patients present with rapid hemodynamic deterioration. 19 Subacute tamponade, as in neoplastic or idiopathic effusions accumulating over days to weeks, may produce very large effusions (>1 L) with only mild hemodynamic compromise because the pericardium gradually accommodates the increasing volume. This distinction has important implications: acute tamponade is managed emergently under Entry Point 2 (Fig. 1 ), while subacute tamponade with moderate hemodynamic compromise may allow time for the scoring-based drainage decision detailed below. Importantly, patients with subacute tamponade are often not hypotensive and may be normotensive or hypertensive on presentation, reflecting a compensatory increase in systemic vascular resistance, likely mediated by neurohormonal activation. 20

Imaging Evaluation TTE is the first-line imaging modality for characterization of effusion size, composition (anechoic transudates versus echogenic or loculated exudates), and hemodynamic impact. TTE and Transesophageal echocardiography provide additional value for complex or loculated effusions, particularly postcardiac surgery. Common mimickers, left pleural effusion (posterior to the descending aorta on parasternal long-axis view) and epicardial fat (echogenic, anterior, moving synchronously with myocardium), should be distinguished at baseline.

Cardiac CT characterizes effusion composition using Hounsfield unit (HU) measurements: transudates (0–20 HU), exudates (20–50 HU), hemorrhagic effusions (>50–60 HU), and chylous effusions (−60 to −80 HU). These ranges are approximate and may overlap; HU values should be interpreted in clinical context and, when available, correlated with fluid analysis. CT also detects pericardial thickening, calcification, and adjacent mediastinal pathology, and guides pericardiocentesis in anatomically complex cases. CMR provides the most comprehensive tissue characterization: T 1 -weighted sequences assess effusion composition, T 2 -STIR detects pericardial edema and active inflammation, and LGE confirms inflammatory activity and predicts response to anti-inflammatory therapy.
Pericardial Effusion Drainage Score

In clinically stable patients with subacute tamponade, the decision to drain the pericardium is guided by a standardized scoring system encompassing three parameters: effusion etiology, effusion size, and echocardiographic hemodynamic assessment (Table 5 ). 21 A total score ≥4 supports consideration of pericardial drainage in the appropriate clinical context. The score should complement, not replace, clinical judgment, particularly in the presence of hemodynamic compromise, high-risk etiologies, or evolving physiology. A surgical score of 4 points, attributable to aortic dissection, purulent effusion, or trauma, necessitates immediate operative intervention rather than needle drainage. The score may evolve over time as effusion size and hemodynamic parameters change; patients with borderline scores require frequent reassessment.

Pericardial Drainage Echo-guided pericardiocentesis using a subxiphoid or para-apical approach is safe and effective for most nonsurgical effusions. 22 Surgical drainage (pericardial window or pericardiectomy) is preferred for loculated effusions, recurrent effusions following pericardiocentesis, traumatic effusion, purulent pericarditis, and aortic dissection. Following drainage, RA pressure must be reassessed; persistent elevation confirms effusive–CP. Medical Management and Follow-Up

Stable small effusions may be managed conservatively with serial imaging. For inflammatory etiologies, NSAIDs plus colchicine are first-line; anti-IL-1 agents or corticosteroids may be escalated as needed. Anti-inflammatory therapy is most appropriate when effusion is accompanied by symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, or imaging evidence of pericardial inflammation. Underlying causes, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, HIV, and malignancy must be identified and treated. In patients with known or suspected malignancy, pericardial effusion may reflect direct tumor involvement, treatment-related inflammation, or infection, and management should be individualized based on hemodynamic status, need for diagnostic confirmation, and overall disease trajectory. 1 For malignant effusions, drainage provides symptom relief and cytological diagnosis, with management directed at the primary malignancy. During active inflammatory disease, CRP should be reassessed serially until normalization and used to guide anti-inflammatory therapy and tapering.
4. INCIDENTAL PERICARDIAL EFFUSION

In patients with moderate-to-large incidental effusions, evaluation should be guided by symptoms, inflammatory markers, and risk factors, with targeted Tier 1 and selective Tier 2 testing as indicated. Broad Tier 2 testing should be reserved for patients without an apparent cause, those with elevated inflammatory markers, or those with high-risk clinical features. If inflammatory markers are elevated without hemodynamic compromise, inflammatory pericarditis with effusion should be considered, while secondary causes such as autoimmune disease, malignancy, infection, renal disease, and hypothyroidism should be excluded. If inflammatory markers are normal and there is no hemodynamic compromise, idiopathic pericardial effusion is the most likely diagnosis; observation with serial imaging is reasonable.

In patients with no obvious etiology and no evidence of hemodynamic compromise, the Pericardial Effusion Drainage Score should be applied if the effusion is moderate-to-large. If a specific treatable cause is identified, it should be addressed directly. A small proportion of patients will have elevations in right-sided pressures after drainage, establishing the diagnosis of effusive-CP and directing subsequent management as outlined above. 5. RIGHT-PREDOMINANT HEART FAILURE: CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS Presentation

CP is characterized by loss of pericardial compliance, resulting in impaired diastolic ventricular filling and a right-predominant heart failure syndrome. Presentation is typically insidious, with progressive fatigue, dyspnea, peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly, and Kussmaul sign (a paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration). Chest pain is often absent. The lungs are characteristically clear, although pleural effusion may be present. Atrial fibrillation occurs in >20% of cases.

CP may arise from irreversible pericardial thickening and fibrosis (chronic/fixed CP), from active pericardial inflammation (transient CP, which may resolve with anti-inflammatory therapy), or as a consequence of effusive-CP. Risk factors are listed in Table 6 . Table 6. High-Risk Conditions for Constrictive Pericarditis High-Risk Conditions for Constrictive Pericarditis • Prior pericarditis (especially recurrent or inadequately treated) • Cardiac surgery or thoracic radiation therapy • Connective tissue disease • HIV • Tuberculosis • Purulent pericarditis Open in a new tab Key Distinction: CP versus Restrictive Cardiomyopathy

Differentiating CP from restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is the most critical diagnostic challenge and requires multimodality evaluation. The defining hemodynamic hallmark of CP is dissociation between intrathoracic and intracardiac pressures during respiration, producing exaggerated interventricular dependence (discordant LV/RV pressure responses to respiration). In RCM, this dissociation is absent, and ventricular pressures change concordantly with respiration. Tissue Doppler annular velocity (medial e’ >8 cm/s and annulus reversus) helps distinguish CP from RCM. Annulus reversus (medial e’ > lateral e’) reflects lateral annular tethering by the pericardium, whereas annular velocities are typically globally reduced in RCM.

Cardiac CT provides anatomic information, including pericardial thickness (>3 mm is abnormal; >6 mm strongly supports CP), calcification distribution (critical for preoperative planning), and effusion characterization by HU values. Normal pericardial thickness does not exclude CP. CMR integrates anatomic and functional assessment. Free-breathing cine sequences demonstrate respirophasic ventricular interdependence; myocardial tagging sequences uniquely demonstrate wall tethering (pericardium and epicardium moving as a unit) and conical ventricular deformity, both specific to pericardial constraint. LGE and T 2 -STIR detect active pericardial inflammation in transient CP. In practice, TTE is used to establish hemodynamic physiology, CT is used when calcification or precise thickness assessment is required, and CMR is used when the diagnosis is equivocal, when myocardial disease must be excluded, or when assessment of inflammatory activity will change management. 23 When noninvasive imaging is inconclusive or discordant with the clinical presentation, invasive hemodynamic assessment may be required to confirm constrictive physiology. Key findings include elevated and near-equalized diastolic pressures (typically within 5 mm Hg), dip-and-plateau (“square root”) ventricular pressure tracings, elevated right atrial pressure, and ventricular discordance on simultaneous LV/RV pressure recording during respiration or respiratory challenge, the latter being the most specific hemodynamic feature of constrictive physiology (Fig. 4 ). 24 Cardiac catheterization remains the reference standard for hemodynamic confirmation when noninvasive imaging is equivocal and is particularly important in presurgical planning.

Subtype Assessment and Management The pathway stratifies CP into three subtypes, each with a distinct management branch (Fig. 4 ): Transient/inflammatory CP: Recent onset, CMR LGE+ and/or T 2 -STIR+, and elevated CRP. Anti-inflammatory therapy is initiated with NSAIDs and colchicine, with corticosteroids or anti-IL-1 agents added as needed, along with diuretics for volume management. Serial CMR at 3–6-month intervals and CRP monitoring assess response. Pericardiectomy is deferred pending response to medical therapy. Effusive–constrictive CP:

Effusive–CP is defined by persistence of constrictive physiology following pericardial drainage, reflected by persistently elevated right atrial pressure and ongoing echocardiographic or hemodynamic features of constriction. This entity is often associated with visceral pericardial inflammation and should prompt assessment for active inflammation to guide therapy. Management mirrors the transient/inflammatory arm; if constriction persists despite optimal medical therapy, pericardiectomy is indicated. Chronic/fixed (“burnt-out”) CP:

Pericardial calcification or significant thickening on CT, CMR LGE−, failure to respond to anti-inflammatory therapy, and NYHA class III–IV or progressive right-sided HF. These patients should be referred to a Pericardial Disease Center and evaluated for radical pericardiectomy at a high-volume surgical center. Surgical treatment should consist of radical pericardiectomy performed at an experienced high-volume center, typically extending from phrenic nerve to phrenic nerve when feasible, and should be reserved for patients with fixed constrictive physiology or persistent constriction despite appropriate anti-inflammatory therapy. 25 Referral for pericardiectomy should occur before the development of advanced end-organ dysfunction, as operative risk increases with progressive hepatic, renal, or nutritional compromise. Palliative care should be offered to patients who are not surgical candidates. 26
CONCLUSIONS

A systematic, pathway-driven approach to pericardial disease provides a framework for clinicians managing a heterogeneous, often diagnostically challenging group of conditions. The CHASER II pathway organizes management around five clinical entry points: chest pain, hemodynamic collapse, dyspnea, incidental effusion, and right-predominant heart failure, each initiating a defined sequence of diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment. Updated evidence supports IL-1 blockade as the preferred escalation strategy for recurrent, incessant, or refractory pericarditis with objective inflammatory activity, with rilonacept supported by the strongest randomized evidence and regulatory approval; CMR remains the key tool for phenotyping and guiding treatment escalation. Additionally, a subtype-based approach to CP is recommended, reserving pericardiectomy for patients who do not respond to medical therapy or present with fixed fibrotic disease. This pathway integrates contemporary evidence into a practical clinical framework that facilitates precise diagnosis, phenotype-driven therapy, and standardized management of pericardial disease.
